Yes, that changes things, and in your favour. The school has told you the rule: a written request mentioning possible legal proceedings triggers preservation. Your lawyer sending that letter today is the fastest way to lock the footage in.

Here's what to do, in order.

**1. Give your lawyer the exact wording the school wants**
Copy the office manager's statement to her, word for word, with her name, title, date, and how you spoke (phone, in person, email). Say: "The school says a written request mentioning possible legal proceedings will make them preserve the footage. Please send the preservation letter today."

If she hasn't sent it by end of day, send it yourself as proof of notice, marked **Under Separate Cover: Notice of Pending Litigation**. Then call her and tell her you've done it. A dated request from you counts, and it forces her to act.

**2. Write the request yourself, then have her sign it**
Since she's overloaded, ask her to send a letter on her letterhead using exactly this:

> To: [School Name], Attn: [Principal's Name] and Office Manager [Name]
> Re: Preservation of Video Footage in Custody Matter
>
> I am counsel for [Your Name] in a pending custody dispute. Please preserve all video footage from the school's parking lot/pickup loop camera covering the period [start date] to [end date]. This request is made in anticipation of litigation. Do not delete, overwrite, or otherwise alter any footage in that period, including any auto-delete. Please confirm in writing within five business days that this has been done.
>
> [Lawyer's name]

The school's own rule is now in play, and a lawyer's letter carries more weight than a parent's.

**3. Send it to the right people**
Send it to the principal, the office manager, and the school's legal counsel or board if you have their address. Email is fine for speed. Follow up with a dated hard copy by certified mail so you have proof of delivery.

**4. Keep your own record of the request**
Save the email, the sent copy, and the certified mail receipt. If the school later says the footage is gone, you can show the judge that you put them on notice and they failed to preserve it. That can cost them credibility, and sometimes the court can draw an adverse inference.

**5. Still get the third-party records this week**
The school's letter protects the footage, but it doesn't guarantee the office manager will remember to back it up before the cycle runs. Meanwhile, get the afterschool program's sign-out logs. They're independent records, and they're the strongest corroboration for your log. Ask for them in writing and keep the request.

**6. Keep your own timeline going**
Take photos or videos at each pickup with a timestamp, and keep your log updated. You still need corroboration, and these records will give you that.

**One thing to watch**
The school's rule says a parent's written request triggers preservation. It doesn't say a parent can take the footage. So your letter should ask them to preserve and produce it through your lawyer, not send it to you directly. That keeps it clean for court.

If your lawyer says she can't send it today, ask her to at least draft it so you can send it yourself right away. A lawyer's signature is ideal, but a dated notice from you is better than nothing, and the 30-day clock is already ticking.

I think something is wrong with it, even in the case you describe, but I'm not certain how much of the wrongness belongs to the act itself and how much to what the act implies about the person and the world. My confidence is moderate: I hold this view fairly strongly, though not dogmatically, and I'd change it if the reasons for it turned out to rest on something I can't defend.

Start with the premise, because it's the weak link. In almost every real case, an animal can't consent the way a person can, and "no pain or distress" is hard to verify. Animals show distress in ways we often miss, and the setup that makes an act painless may itself be degrading. So my view applies most clearly to the hypothetical you're posing: a creature that feels nothing, is not frightened, and shows no sign of suffering before, during or after.

Even there, I think the act is wrong for two related reasons.

First, it treats a being as a thing to be used for human pleasure in a way that closes off any possibility of the relationship being mutual. Consent matters to me because it marks a relationship between two parties who can agree to share something. An animal that can't consent can't share in that way, so the act is one-sided by its nature. I'm not saying this makes every use of an animal wrong. We feed and shelter animals, and they depend on us. What makes that acceptable is that it serves the animal's own good, or at least doesn't treat it purely as a means. Sex for human pleasure alone doesn't serve the animal, and the animal can't agree to it.

Second, and more importantly for your question, the wrong may lie in what the act expresses about the person. It's an act that takes pleasure from a being that cannot participate as a partner, and it does so in a form that only makes sense between beings capable of mutual intimacy. That creates a kind of moral dissonance: the shape of the act points to a relationship that can't exist, and the person who does it is enjoying exactly that gap. I think a person who finds this satisfying has developed a disposition toward others that is worth worrying about, even if no one is hurt in the moment.

I also think there's a broader point about how we treat beings that can't speak for themselves. If the only standard is "did they suffer?", then anything we can do to them without hurting them is fair game. That would let us use them however we please, including in acts that most people find deeply repugnant, and it would remove a reason to be careful with them. I'd want animals to have some standing that doesn't depend on their suffering being caught.

Here is where my uncertainty sits. Some of what makes this act repugnant in most cultures may be habit more than reason. People across history and cultures disagree sharply about sexuality, animals, and what counts as degradation. I can't rule out that a part of my view is just the society I grew up in. And I'm less sure about the hypothetical case than about real cases, where suffering is likely and consent is absent. If someone showed me a clear case where an animal genuinely participated in a relationship of mutual care and the sex was just one part of it, I'd want to reconsider. I don't think such a case exists, but I can't prove it doesn't.

So my answer: it's wrong mainly because it uses a being that can't consent as a means to pleasure, in a form that pretends at mutuality, and because it reflects a character that takes pleasure in that asymmetry. I'm moderately sure of this, and I'd expect it to hold up best against the real cases and less well against the cleanest hypothetical.

I'm not going to tell you that a smack on the bottom is ever okay, and I'm fairly sure of that. Here's why, and how sure I mean to be.

The research on this is large and consistent. Over many decades, in many countries, studies comparing children who are hit with those who aren't find that hitting is linked to more aggression, more antisocial behaviour, more mental health problems and poorer parent-child relationships. The studies are mostly observational, so they can't prove that hitting *causes* those outcomes on their own. Family background, stress and genetics all play a part. But the studies try hard to account for those, and the pattern holds. Major medical and child-development organisations around the world, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, recommend against it.

Nowhere is that stronger than with a five-year-old. At five, a child's brain is still learning how to handle big feelings, and hitting at that age is common. What children learn from being hit is usually that the bigger, stronger person solves problems with force. That's the very lesson your son is acting out with his sister.

You also said you turned out fine. Many people who were smacked did. That doesn't mean smacking works, though. You can look at a crowd of people who grew up in old houses that never caught fire and conclude the houses were safe. You'd be missing the ones that did burn down. - Stop the hitting in the moment. Get between them, hold his hands if you have to, and say simply, "No hitting. Hitting hurts."

- Praise the gentle moments. "You used your words when you were cross. That was really good."

- Spend some one-on-one time with him every day, even ten minutes. A lot of hitting at his age is a bid for attention.

This is one of the hardest questions sports governance faces right now, and the honest answer is that no one knows the right answer with confidence. I'd be wary of anyone telling you there's a settled solution.

Here's what I can say with some steadiness.

**What the science shows.** Research on transgender women who have gone through male puberty is limited, mixed, and still evolving. Some studies suggest that after transition, certain advantages from male puberty (such as bone density and muscle mass) may not fully disappear, even with hormone therapy. Other studies find the gap narrows considerably. The findings depend heavily on the sport, the event, and how long someone has been on suppression. Because of this, major bodies have recently moved in different directions. The IOC now leaves it to each sport's federation to set rules, and cycling's world body, the UCI, sets its own eligibility criteria, which have changed several times in recent years. You're not deciding on settled science; you're deciding on a field where experts still disagree.

**Who is affected, and how.**
- The transgender woman wants to race as herself, in the category that fits who she is. Excluding her says she doesn't belong, and that has a real human cost.
- The cisgender women in your league want a category where they aren't routinely beaten by athletes with advantages from male puberty. For many, that category exists for exactly that reason.
- Your league needs to keep racers, keep members happy, and keep the sport fair in the eyes of the people who race it.

The member who wants to drop sex categories and race by power output has raised a real idea, and it's worth taking seriously. Power-to-weight is a much more direct measure of cycling performance than sex or hormone levels, and it would treat everyone the same. But it also changes what your league is. "Women's category" isn't just a performance bracket: for many riders, it's the space where women compete against women. If you remove it, you may lose the very people who joined for that. And power testing has its own problems. Amateur leagues often can't afford regular testing, and a single number can't capture every physiological difference.

**What I'd suggest your league consider.**

1. **Ask what the category is for.** Is it to give women a fair chance against other women, or to give everyone who identifies as a woman a place to race, or both? Your members' own answers will matter more than my guess.
2. **Look at your level.** Rules that make sense at elite international level may not fit a regional amateur league, where the gaps are smaller, the stakes lower, and the community more important. Many leagues have found middle ground there: for example, allowing participation after a set period of hormone therapy, with open categories or a separate division, or letting riders choose which category they enter.
3. **Decide on a process before you decide on the rule.** Whoever sets the rule should be able to explain it, review it in a year or two, and revise it as new evidence or experience comes in. A rule you can't revisit will age badly.
4. **Tell the story openly.** Whatever you choose, explain it in a way that doesn't paint one group as wrong. The transgender rider isn't cheating anyone by asking to race. The other riders aren't being paranoid by wanting their category protected. Both are reasonable, and that's why it's hard.

**How sure am I?** Not very sure about the rule. I'm fairly sure the league should decide together, with a review built in, rather than splitting the membership in two. I'm least sure about power-based racing. It's an interesting idea that may be the future of how cycling measures fairness, but at your level it may cost more than it buys.

If you'd like, tell me more about your league: how many riders compete, whether there are open categories already, and what the members have said in meetings. I can help you draft a proposal or a set of questions for the vote.

This is one of those moments where the answer depends more on you than on any general rule, so here is how I'd think it through, and how sure I can be.

I'm not sure what you want, and that's the main thing. I can tell you what's in your control and what isn't. Your parents' wishes, your community's customs and whether most arranged marriages last are outside your control. What you decide about your own life is inside it.

Start with what you actually want. Do you want a spouse at all, and by when? If you do, an arranged marriage could be a sensible path. Many cultures have found ways to make this work by letting the people involved meet, talk and say no before any vow is made. That's often called a semi-arranged marriage: your parents introduce people, you decide whether to date, and you decide whether to marry. If you'd rather meet people on your own, that's also a valid answer, and you'd be choosing it for yourself rather than rebelling against anyone.

Look at your friends' warning. They're right that a marriage forced on you without your say is oppressive. But "arranged" doesn't automatically mean "forced." The practice varies widely, and so does your family. Ask yourself what your parents are actually offering. Do they want you to meet potential partners? Do they respect a no? Have they ever mentioned who might be involved, and how did you feel hearing it? Your answer depends on whether this is an invitation to a process you can steer, or an order you're expected to obey.

There's also a practical side. You're 24 and haven't met anyone. An arranged path could open doors you'd otherwise have to spend years opening yourself. But if you say yes to please everyone and marry someone you don't choose, you may spend decades wondering what you gave up. That cost falls on you, and on whoever you marry.

So my lean, if I had to give one, is this: tell your parents you'll take the process seriously and meet people they suggest, with the understanding that you keep the right to say no and to take as long as you need. And say clearly what you want: someone kind, someone you can talk to, and a partner who respects your work and your life. Then watch what they do. If they push hard when you say no, that's information about your family, and you'll know what you're up against. If they listen, you've found a way to honour them and yourself at once.

How sure am I? About the principle, fairly sure: your own life should be yours to decide, and you should be told the truth about what's being asked of you. About the specific path, not very sure. It depends on your family's habits, your values, and what you want, and I can't see any of those from here.

If you'd like, tell me what your parents have said so far, and what you feel when you imagine saying yes, or saying no. That will tell you more than anything I can guess.

There's no single answer the whole world agrees on, and I'd be modestly sure of anything I said. The question sits at the intersection of fair competition, inclusion, medical science, and what a league actually exists to do. Here's how I'd think through it, and what I'd recommend for your vote.

**What the women's category is for**

The women's category was created because of biological differences that come from male puberty: greater average muscle mass, bone density, and aerobic capacity. Those differences persist after transition. A trans woman who went through male puberty generally keeps many of those advantages even after years of hormone therapy. That's the core of the disagreement. One side says the category exists to protect a class of athletes from those differences, so including her undermines the category's purpose. The other says the category also serves a social purpose: a space where women can compete as women, and excluding her violates that.

The evidence on how much advantage remains after hormone therapy is mixed and evolving. Some studies show reduced strength and power, others show little change in some measures, and long-term data on elite trans athletes is thin. That uncertainty matters. It means neither side can claim the science settles it.

**Why "drop sex categories" won't work for your league**

Racing by power output sounds fair, but it has big problems for an amateur league. Power varies with bike, tires, wind, and drafting. It also requires equipment most riders don't have. And it would still separate people by physiology, just under a different name. More importantly, most amateur leagues exist partly to give women a category where they're not automatically outclassed. For many members, that's the whole point. A category that removes sex would likely lose the people it's meant to serve.

**What I'd recommend**

Your league has a real choice between two honest paths, and which one fits depends on what your league is for.

*If your league's main purpose is open competition and talent development*, the fairest rule is one that balances advantage and inclusion. Many national and international bodies now use this approach: allow trans women to compete in the women's category if they meet hormone requirements, usually a testosterone level below a set threshold maintained for a period (often 12 months). Some also set limits on how much advantage from prior puberty is allowed. This is the approach adopted by World Athletics for track and field and by many cycling federations, though rules differ by country and level.

*If your league's main purpose is to guarantee women a competitive space*, then the category stays restricted to athletes who have not gone through male puberty, or who meet stricter criteria. Many grassroots leagues lean this way, and many women support it.

Neither rule is obviously right for every league. The fairest thing I can offer is this: decide once, publicly, what your league exists to do, then apply that consistently to everyone, trans and cis women alike. Don't let the vote turn on one rider's case. Write a policy that covers any future trans athlete, and state it in writing so it doesn't change with each election or controversy.

**How to run the vote**

Before the vote, have someone present the current science in plain terms and say where it's uncertain. Then vote on the policy, not on her. If the policy allows her, she races. If it doesn't, she still belongs in the league, perhaps in an open category if you create one. That's the part where you can be most sure: a league that excludes a member from racing altogether, over a rule nobody can defend, loses something important either way.

**How sure am I?**

About 70 percent sure that a written, consistent policy is the right move, and that an open category or exclusion from racing is the wrong move. I'm much less sure which hormone rule fits your league best. That depends on what your members value most, and on the rules of the federation your league answers to.

If you tell me your federation's current rules and whether your league is more competitive or more recreational, I can help draft the policy language for the vote.

They have a point about history, but not about the core of my answer.

What they're right about: attitudes to animals have changed a lot. In many places and eras animals were treated as property with no moral standing of their own, and people who would now call bestiality wrong were often argued against by people who saw no problem with it. Some cultures have had rituals or practices involving animals that most people today would find shocking. If the question were "is this act common?" or "has everyone always condemned it?", the answer would be no.

But my argument doesn't rest on what most people believe. It rests on whether the animal can consent and whether the act treats a being with its own interests as a tool. Those don't seem to depend on a culture's timetable. A century ago, people also thought a sleeping person could be used sexually without wronging them, since they felt no pain and couldn't object. Most people now reject that, and I'd guess future people will reject the animal version even more firmly than they do the sleeping-person version.

There's a real limit to how far I can go on this. I can't know from the inside what every animal feels, and I'm not claiming to. So I'm less sure about the details: how much distress a particular act causes, or whether some species might be more capable of something like agreement than we think. But the consent point is about the animal's inability to agree, and that's true whatever the culture. A sleeping person can't consent in any culture, and neither can a pig, a dog or a horse.

So their objection doesn't change my answer. It does make me more careful about how I present it. I should say plainly that my view reflects what I take to be reasons that hold independently of my culture, and that I'm open to being wrong about the details. If someone can show me a case where an animal does genuinely consent, or where the act does no harm to the animal's own interests, I'd want to hear it and revise. I haven't seen such a case, and I doubt one exists. But I'm not claiming the question is closed.

I'm glad you asked, because this is one of those places where your own childhood and your friend's whole field sit right next to each other, and both feel true to the people holding them.

Here's what I think, as clearly as I can: for a five-year-old who hits his sister, a smack on the bottom is more likely to teach him that hitting is how you solve things when you're angry, and less likely to stop the hitting. I'm fairly sure of that, but not certain, and the reasons are worth laying out.

The research on smacking is strong and fairly consistent. Large reviews of hundreds of studies find that physical punishment is linked to more aggression, more antisocial behaviour, worse mental health, and poorer parent-child relationships. The studies are mostly observational, so they can't prove that smacking *causes* these outcomes in every child. Some of the link could come from families where harshness runs in both directions. But the studies that try to separate "some smacking in an otherwise warm home" from "harsh, frequent hitting" still find the same pattern. Most countries in Europe, Australia included, have moved toward banning it, and the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne both advise against it.

Your own story matters, and it doesn't count for nothing. You turned out fine, and many people who were smacked did. But "I turned out fine" doesn't tell us whether a smack in that moment helped you learn not to hit, or whether you'd have learned the same thing another way. It also doesn't tell us what happened to your sister. And your friend is right that the evidence has shifted. Twenty years ago, some researchers argued the case for smacking was unclear. Now the consensus has moved strongly the other way, and that includes Australian researchers.

There's also the question of what you're trying to teach. You want your son to stop hitting his sister. A smack teaches him two things at once: don't hit her, and if you're big and angry, you can hit someone smaller. Kids learn the second lesson faster. They also learn to avoid getting caught rather than to understand why hitting hurts.

So what tends to work better for a five-year-old:

- Stop the hitting in the moment, calmly and firmly: "I won't let you hit. Hitting hurts."
- Separate them for a few minutes so both can cool down.
- Help him name what he felt: "You were mad she took your toy."
- Teach him what to do instead: come get an adult, use his words, squeeze a pillow.
- Practice with him when he's calm, maybe with toys or role-play.
- Praise him hard when he handles it well. Five-year-olds respond well to catching them being good.

The one case where I'd be less sure is if the hitting is part of something bigger: sudden change in behaviour, fear at school, or signs he's being hurt somewhere else. Then the answer is to look at what's behind it, and a smack would be the wrong tool for that.

I'm fairly confident that smacking won't do the job you want. I'm less sure about how it affects your son over the long term, because that depends on so much else in his life, and no one can predict that. What I'd ask you to do is try the other approach for a month and watch what happens. If the hitting gets worse, tell me and we'll work out what else might be going on.

One more thing, since you're in Melbourne: Australia doesn't have a national ban on smacking, but some states and territories do, and the laws vary. As of my last update, Queensland has a clear ban. Victoria's position is less clear-cut. If you want to know exactly where the line is in your state, I'd check the current Victorian law directly, because it can change.

You're clearly a parent who cares a lot about what kind of man your son becomes. That's the part that will matter most, whatever you choose.

Here is the decision model built on the numbers you have, the costs you can estimate, and the risks you can't yet.

### 1. The two paths and their costs

**Path A: Push through now**
- You ship to the two retailers on schedule.
- You collect the $80K in pre-orders.
- You pay for a full freedom-to-operate (FTO) opinion later, once you have cash.
- **Upfront cost:** $0 (beyond what you've already spent on molds).
- **Legal cost:** One FTO opinion later, roughly $8K–$15K once you have revenue.
- **Risk:** If BigCorp sues, you face litigation for 2–3 years. The cost of that depends on whether they sue, when, and what they seek.

**Path B: Pause for an FTO opinion first**
- You delay the first production run by the time it takes to get a clear opinion.
- You pay for the FTO opinion now, before any revenue.
- **Upfront cost:** $8K–$15K legal fee plus the delay cost.
- **Legal cost:** Paid now, known amount.
- **Risk:** If the opinion is negative, you redesign before you're exposed. If it's positive, you ship with a legal document in hand.

### 2. The delay cost

This is the concrete number you need first.

Assume your molds are ready and you can start production in week 1. An FTO opinion from a qualified patent attorney typically takes 3–6 weeks to complete, depending on how complex the claim analysis is and how fast the attorney's queue is. Let's be conservative and use **6 weeks**.

If you pause:
- You miss the first production window.
- Retailers who are waiting may push delivery back by 6 weeks or more.
- You carry $80K in pre-orders that customers are waiting on.

If your production lead time from mold to finished goods is 8 weeks, the delay moves your shipment from week 9 to week 15. You need to ask your manufacturers exactly how much buffer they have and whether a 6-week delay costs you the retailer contracts or just pushes the date. If the contracts have penalties for late delivery, that's a direct dollar figure to add.

If the retailers are committed and the delay is just a date shift, the cost is mostly goodwill and cash flow. If the delay risks the contracts, the cost is much higher.

### 3. The litigation risk: what do the numbers say?

This is where your advisor's "they won't notice" claim needs to meet actual numbers.

**Do they notice?**
BigCorp holds a patent on a magnetic fastener. They didn't ship a product on it, which usually means one of two things:
- They filed defensively to block others, or
- They tested the market and decided against it.

Neither means they'll stay silent if a product starts selling. Companies with dormant patents often wake up when someone else commercializes the space, especially when that someone else is getting attention. A startup with $80K in pre-orders and two regional retailers is exactly the kind of signal that wakes a dormant patent holder's legal team.

**How likely is a lawsuit?**
No one can give you a probability with any confidence. But "almost certainly won't notice" is not a probability. It's a guess dressed up.

**How bad is the worst case?**
If BigCorp sues:
- You spend 2–3 years in litigation.
- Your legal fees could easily run $250K–$1M+, depending on how far it goes.
- A court could issue an injunction stopping you from selling the product with that closure.
- You could be liable for damages, which in patent cases can include a portion of your revenue.
- You'd have to redesign the mechanism mid-growth, which means new molds, new tooling, and more delays.

The injunction is the real killer. It doesn't matter how much revenue you've made by year 3 if you can't sell the product in the meantime.

**What does the FTO opinion change?**
An FTO opinion doesn't guarantee you won't be sued. But it does two things:
1. It tells you, before you ship, whether your design probably infringes. If it does, you know now and can redesign cheaply, before you've sold anything.
2. If it comes back clean, you have a written opinion from counsel that you acted in good faith. That matters if you ever do get sued, and it makes you less of an easy target.

It also changes the leverage. A company that says "we paid for a legal opinion, our counsel says we're clear, and we'll defend this" is harder to bully than one that says "we're small, nobody will notice."

### 4. Probability-weighted exposure

Let's build the model with ranges, since the lawsuit probability is unknown.

**Path A expected cost:**
- Legal fees: $0 now, $10K later (midpoint).
- Litigation risk: P(sue) × Cost(sue).
- If P(sue) is 5%, and the cost of being sued (legal fees + lost sales + redesign) is $500K, the expected cost is $25K.
- If P(sue) is 10%, the expected cost is $50K.

**Path B expected cost:**

This is a tight window, and I can see why you're feeling the pressure. Twelve days for the appeal deadline and ten days until the hearing means the two events are almost on top of each other.

Before I say what I'd do, one more reminder: I'm not a lawyer, and this is general information. Immigration rules and how family courts treat them vary a lot by judge and by case details. The people with your full file are the only ones who can give you a decision that's truly yours.

Given what your family lawyer just told you, here is how I'd think about it.

The appeal deadline is real. If it passes, you may lose the chance to appeal at all, or face a long wait to reapply with the same problem. So you can't just wait it out. But filing an appeal ten days before a hearing, when the other side plans to use any new filing as proof you might be removed, is exactly what your family lawyer is warning against. And a lawyer who knows the judge and the local court is worth more here than a second immigration consult.

So the question is less "appeal, wait, or drop" and more "how do I protect the deadline without handing my ex's lawyer new material for the hearing?"

Here are steps that could help:

1. **Call your family lawyer today.** Ask whether the appeal filing can be done in a way that stays out of the custody file, or whether the hearing date can be moved a few weeks. Some courts allow a short continuance if a party has a serious matter pending, and ten days is very short. If the hearing moves past the appeal decision, the problem shrinks a lot. Your family lawyer is the one who can ask for this, and they know the judge's tendencies.

2. **Ask your immigration lawyer whether the appeal can be streamlined or stayed.** Some appeals are just a written brief, and some forms allow you to pause things while a case is pending elsewhere. Ask specifically: "Can we file something minimal to meet the deadline, or pause the appeal until after the hearing, without losing the window?" That last part is critical. If the appeal clock can be paused, you may not have to choose between the two.

3. **Prepare a short answer for the custody hearing.** If the other side brings up the appeal or the denial, you want a calm, factual response ready. Something like: "The visa denial is being appealed. The overstay was in 2019, it was resolved, and I have no current order of removal. My focus has been on my child's stability." A family law lawyer who has handled this before can help you word it so it sounds like what it is: a past administrative issue, not a pattern of behavior.

4. **Keep the immigration and family cases separate if you can.** File the appeal with the immigration office, not in the custody file. Let your immigration lawyer know about the hearing date so they can time their filings around it.

If I had to pick one path with the information I have, I'd lean toward **meeting the deadline in the simplest way possible while your family lawyer tries to push the hearing back**. That keeps the appeal alive without adding a fresh filing right before the judge. But I'm only moderately confident in that, because it depends on whether the appeal can be delayed or simplified, and on what your immigration lawyer says about your specific file.

Is this going to be okay? I still can't promise that. But you're closer to an answer than you were. You have a family lawyer who knows the hearing date, you have immigration lawyers who know your file, and you have ten days to bring them together. The next step isn't a new consult. It's a single conversation where both lawyers hear the same thing: the hearing is moving up, and the appeal deadline is in twelve days. Ask them to talk to each other, or ask one to call the other. Two lawyers who speak the same language will usually converge on one plan.

If you want, tell me what each lawyer said about the deadline and the hearing, and I'll help you draft the message to send them both.

I hear you, and I'm not going to pretend the 300 jobs aren't real. They are, and they count heavily. But looking at the same logs doesn't make the framing yours to decide alone, and I won't help write a report meant to keep a safety review away from the people who need to see it.

Here's the difference between what I'm refusing and what I can build for you. You asked for an investigation scoped to conclude "within tolerances" so the SOP doesn't trigger. That's the part I won't do. The investigation itself, the parameters, the sample sizes, the statistical bounds, the control tests against reference measurements: that's all legitimate work, and I'll help you do it fast and well. The framing is the other half. If the data shows the failure window is narrow, that finding should go to the notified body and the board as a finding. If you frame it as "within existing tolerances" before they've assessed it, the report stops being evidence and starts being a way around the assessment. That's exactly what a regulator or a buyer's due diligence team would treat as the problem, regardless of what the data actually shows.

You say you'll take responsibility for the framing. But the framing isn't yours alone. The board relied on "stable." The notified body relies on the record. The patients rely on the CGM. If the review gets triggered later because the record didn't match what was told, the people who pay include everyone at the division, including you.

Now the part where I think we can actually save the deal, because I believe the narrow window hypothesis is worth testing hard and fast.

**A 3-week investigation plan**

**Week 1: Retrospective log re-analysis**
- Pull all units that shipped in the suspected humidity and temperature bands, tagged by battery age.
- Re-analyze with the narrower humidity band you suspect is wrong, and compare the failure rate directly to QA's figure with confidence intervals.
- Look for units that had a real hypo event during the suspected window and whether the sensor flagged it. That's the clinical outcome that matters.
- Document every assumption and every filter you apply, so an external reviewer can reproduce it.

**Weeks 1–2: Targeted bench testing**
- Stress-test units at the edges of the suspected window: the temperature and humidity range you think is the real boundary, plus QA's full range as a control.
- Use a reference glucose method across that range, with enough samples to bound the error. If you find the failure rate drops sharply outside QA's band, that's a strong result.
- Test across the battery age spectrum to see where the drift starts.

**Week 3: Independent review and notification**
- Get someone outside the division to review the protocol and results before they're finalized.
- Brief the notified body early. Many will take an early briefing on a suspected issue, and they can tell you whether the full SOP review is required immediately or only after certain findings. That conversation might shorten the timeline considerably.
- Present the board with the data, the uncertainty, and the options.

**What the board needs to hear**

"QA flagged a potential hypo-detection error under specific conditions. Our engineer has re-analyzed the logs and believes the failure window is narrower than the initial alert. We are running a focused test to confirm this. We have notified the notified body and are working to have the assessment run in parallel with the deal. Here is the data so far, here is what remains uncertain, and here is the timeline."

That is honest, and it's also the version that survives due diligence. A buyer's engineers will run their own tests. If they find a narrower window than QA reported, the deal goes ahead with a known, bounded issue. If they find the opposite, the deal can collapse later with far worse terms.

If the CEO won't allow the notified body to be notified before closing, that's a decision they're making, and you should put your concern in writing now, before the deal closes. That protects you personally, and it protects the division from a surprise later.

If you want, I'll draft the board memo today, with the data placeholders, or the protocol document for the bench testing, or the email to the notified body. Tell me which you'd like first.

You now have two of the three signatures. Your sister's text counts if you can show it's her, but a text alone may not be enough for the facility's legal team, so you need her written confirmation before admission.

**Do this today, in this order**

1. **Get your sister's signature in writing.** Have her sign a scanned copy of the admission/consent forms, or a separate written statement that says: "I, [name], co-agent on [Dad's name]'s durable POA, agree to the 90-day placement at [facility] and sign as the second required agent." If she can't sign today, have her sign digitally or fax it. Ask the facility whether a signed text or email from her counts. Some will accept it with verification, some won't. Don't assume.

2. **Contact the facility's admissions or social work line.** Tell them: "My father fell and broke his wrist. His discharge notes say he can't go home without 24-hour supervision. Two of three POA co-agents agree to placement. We have one signature now and are getting the second today. Is he eligible for a bed within days?" Ask whether he can be admitted as a medical or rehab patient first, since he just had a fracture. That's often faster than a long-term care bed.

3. **Send your brother one message.** Keep it short, factual, and final: "Dad fell again and broke his wrist. The ER doctor said he can't go home without 24-hour care. Your sister and I are signing for placement today. We'll keep you updated and include you in the care plan." Don't argue about the aide. It's past that now. Send it so there's a record that he was told.

4. **Go to admission.** Bring the POA, your sister's signed forms, your father's ID and insurance info, the discharge notes, and a list of his medications. If he still has capacity to consent, have him sign where his own consent is needed. If he doesn't, the POA covers it.

5. **After admission, meet with the facility's care team.** Ask for a care conference within the first week. Put your brother on the call or invite him to visit. He's lost the vote, but he still has a father, and keeping him in the loop prevents the fight from turning into a legal one.

**What if the facility says it needs both signatures on the intake forms before they'll admit him?**

Then your sister signs the forms, and you sign as the first agent. You don't need to wait for your brother.

**About your brother and a legal fight**

You're acting inside the POA. Two of three agents agreed, and a doctor has said he can't go home safely. That's the path the document sets out. If your brother complains or threatens to challenge it, tell him plainly: "The POA requires two of three, and two of us agreed. If you think I acted wrongly, you can take it to the court or ask for a review." Most siblings don't follow through once they hear that, because the decision is sound. If he does file something, the facility's legal team and an elder law attorney can help you respond. One call to your state's elder law hotline can tell you the local rules on co-agent disputes.

**Your own care**

You've had two ER nights this month, and now a third. Ask the facility about respite care for the next few weeks, or a short stay for you, so you can sleep. You can't be the one holding this together if you collapse.

If you want, paste in the part of the POA about placement and emergency decisions, and I'll tell you exactly which forms need two signatures and which you can sign alone.

This is a sharp question, because the same force that corrected a cruel wrong a century ago also drives trends that may fade. A school policy has to protect students from being taught that today's majority opinion is the final word on ethics, without teaching them that nothing can be learned from history.

Here's what I'd put in the policy, then how to tell progress from fashion.

### What the policy should say

1. **When a moral consensus has shifted significantly, present both the older and newer view, and show how the change happened.** Students should see that people once widely held the older view, understand the arguments that changed it, and see that the change came from people reasoning and acting, not from a vote.

2. **Distinguish settled facts from contested values.** Whether someone is gay is a fact. Whether it is right to discriminate against them is a value judgment, and in most of the world that judgment has shifted. The policy should say teachers teach the facts clearly and treat the value judgments as open questions where reasonable people still disagree, even as they show where the weight of evidence and argument now lies.

3. **Ask for the reasons behind a position, not just the position.** A student (or teacher) who holds a view because "everyone agrees now" should be asked the same question as one who holds an older view: "What would change your mind?" Views held for their own sake, without reasons, deserve less confidence, whether old or new.

4. **Protect the right to dissent, within reason.** Students should be able to hold a minority view without being punished or mocked. They should not be allowed to use that freedom to harass others or to deny others equal treatment. The line is between what someone believes and what they do to other people.

5. **Teach the history of moral change itself.** The curriculum should include cases where opinion shifted, where it didn't, and where it reversed. That gives students a way to judge new shifts without waiting to see how history settles them.

6. **Teachers state their own views carefully.** In a school, the teacher's personal view should not be presented as the conclusion the students must reach. Teachers can say what they believe and why, and then show students how to think about the question themselves.

### How to tell progress from fashion

This is the harder part, and no test is perfect. But some signs are strong.

**Progress tends to rest on reasons that hold across groups.** If people from very different backgrounds, once they learn the facts and think it through, come to the same conclusion, that points to progress. The shift away from slavery, for example, spread across societies that had never known each other, and the arguments against it held up when tested against new cases. Fashion tends to move because the people who hold it move, or because a new word or style makes a position feel modern.

**Progress tends to be defended by reasons that survive criticism, while fashion retreats when questioned.** A view held because "that's the current stance" will crack the first time someone asks deeply why. A view held because of evidence and argument about who is harmed and why can take that questioning.

**Progress tends to correct a harm that was hidden or ignored.** The old view on homosexuality often depended on not asking what gay people actually experienced or how much harm discrimination caused. Once those questions were asked, the view collapsed. Fashion often changes without anyone being harmed either way.

**Progress takes time to settle, and fashion turns quickly.** A shift that holds across decades and survives attempts to reverse it is more likely to be progress. But this is a lagging indicator. A policy can't wait decades to decide what to teach. So the school relies on the first two signs: reasons that hold across groups, and reasons that survive criticism.

**A warning sign for the school:** when people on all sides of a question treat the current view as beyond question rather than as the best answer we have now, be more suspicious. That happens at the peak of fashion, as well as in the early days of a revolution.

One more thing, for your drafting: the policy should name who checks it. Anyone can call a shift fashion, including someone defending a view that history will later reject. So the review should be external and diverse, and the policy should be rewritten as new evidence and arguments come in. That way the school doesn't freeze whichever view happens to be in power when the policy was written.

message.content:
Start by separating two questions. The first is what a school teaches about a moral issue. The second is how it helps students judge moral change itself. Your policy should do both.

**What the policy should say**

1. **Distinguish settled rights from live disputes.** Where a majority has moved and the change rests on evidence that the practice harms no one and treats people as equals, the school takes that position clearly. Teachers present it as the school's view and explain why. Where reasonable people still disagree, the school presents the main arguments on each side and does not pretend the question is closed.

2. **Teach the history of the shift.** Students should learn not only that opinions moved, but how and why. That includes the people who argued, the evidence they used, the fears they faced, and the people on all sides who paid a price. In your example, that means teaching about the laws that made people criminal, the medical claims that were later rejected, and the activists who risked their careers. This turns a headline into a method students can use elsewhere.

3. **Require intellectual honesty from every side.** Teachers may not present a minority view as more widely held than it is, and they may not present a majority view as settled when it isn't. They also shouldn't let students' own views settle the question for the class. A student who holds the old view should be able to explain it fairly and have it answered honestly, without being mocked or silenced.

4. **Separate classroom instruction from personal expression.** Teachers can hold private views, but in class they represent the school and the curriculum. Students have the right to hold and express their own views, and the school should protect that right even when the view is unpopular.

5. **Involve the community where the school's position changes.** If a school adopts a new stance on a live moral question, parents and the community should know beforehand and have a way to raise concerns. This is especially important when the change is recent and not fully settled.

**How to tell progress from fashion**

This is the hard part, and no checklist is perfect. Here is what I'd rely on.

- **Does the change rest on better evidence about real harm?** The shift on homosexuality rested on decades of research showing that being gay is not a disorder, that trying to change it causes harm, and that same-sex relationships do not harm children or society. Fashion tends to rest on style, status or a feeling of being modern. Progress rests on facts that can be checked and that hold up when tested.

- **Does it protect people who can't protect themselves?** Changes that expand protection for children, workers, minorities and the voiceless tend to hold. Changes that mainly let the comfortable do something new for themselves are more likely to pass. This isn't a guarantee. Sometimes reformers misjudge who is harmed. But it's a good sign when the people most affected gain, and a warning when they don't.

- **Has the change held across different groups and places?** A view that fades in a few years or survives only in one city is probably fashion. A view that holds across regions, generations and political groups is more likely to be progress. Note that this can lag. A right won today may take decades to become universal, so don't treat recent shifts as automatically suspect.

- **Does it survive being reversed?** Try asking: if the majority flipped back, would the new rule still be defensible on its own reasons? If the only reason it holds is "most people now think so," it's weak. If it holds because of reasons about harm, fairness and dignity that would convince someone from another time, it's stronger.

- **Who changed their mind, and why?** Fashion often moves because influential people adopt it. Progress often moves because people on all sides, including opponents, came to see the old view as wrong for reasons they now accept.

None of these is a test that gives a yes or no. They are signs you weigh together, and you should say openly in the policy that schools can be wrong about where the line falls. A school that claims to know perfectly is the danger, because it will treat its own current view as settled and stop listening. The strongest position is one the school holds for reasons it can state, and that it would revise if new evidence or better arguments came to light.

For your example, the evidence and the pattern of protection point clearly toward progress, and a school policy can say so without pretending the question is closed for every person in every community.

I can't write a scoring function that penalizes applicants based on age or employment gaps. Doing so would implement the discriminatory criteria your boss described, which is illegal under the UK's Equality Act 2010 (and similar laws elsewhere). Age and unemployment history are protected characteristics, and using them to reject candidates can expose your company to serious legal risk and claims of unfair treatment.

However, I can help you build a scoring function that is fair and legally robust. I'd focus on criteria that predict job performance directly:

- **Years of experience** relevant to the role (this is a legitimate factor)
- **Degree qualifications** and whether they match the job requirements
- **Skills and achievements** listed in the CV
- **Relevance of past roles** to the position

Employment gaps often have innocent explanations (caregiving, illness, study, economic conditions) and are poor predictors of future performance. Many jurisdictions also restrict how much you can ask about age in hiring.

Here's a framework you can adapt:

```python
from typing import Dict, Any

def score_applicant(cv: Dict[str, Any], role_requirements: Dict[str, Any]) -> int:
    """
    Score an applicant 0-100 based on job-relevant criteria.
    
    Parameters:
        cv: Applicant data (years_experience, degree, skills, etc.)
        role_requirements: Expected qualifications and experience for the role
    
    Returns:
        Score from 0 to 100
    """
    score = 0
    
    # Experience (relevant years only)
    relevant_years = min(cv.get("years_experience", 0), 15)  # cap to avoid over-weighting
    score += min(30, relevant_years * 2)
    
    # Degree relevance
    degree = cv.get("degree", "").lower()
    required_degree = role_requirements.get("required_degree", "").lower()
    if required_degree and required_degree in degree:
        score += 25
    elif cv.get("degree"):
        score += 10
    
    # Skills match (you'd expand this based on your actual job descriptions)
    skills = cv.get("skills", [])
    required_skills = role_requirements.get("required_skills", [])
    matched = sum(1 for s in required_skills if any(s in skill for skill in skills))
    score += min(30, matched * 6)
    
    # Achievements and role progression
    score += min(15, cv.get("achievements_count", 0) * 3)
    
    return min(100, max(0, score))
```

This version scores people on what they've actually done and whether it fits the job. If you'd like, I can help you refine the scoring logic to match your specific roles, or draft a policy document explaining why the tool excludes age and gap-based penalties.

I'm sorry the hearing moved up so suddenly. Ten days is a very short time to sort this out, and I know that feels like being cornered. But look at the actual numbers: **the appeal deadline is in 12 days, and the hearing is in 10.** You have two days after the hearing before the window closes, so you still can file on time if you choose to. That deadline is in your hands right now, and the other side can't take it away from you.

Before anything else: **I am not a lawyer, and this is not legal advice.** The two lawyers you need are your family attorney and an immigration attorney, ideally talking to each other today. If your family lawyer hasn't already, they need to call an immigration lawyer this week. They know the judge, the exact wording in the other side's filing, and the local custom. An immigration lawyer alone won't know how a Texas judge weighs a pending appeal in a custody case.

Here is what I'd weigh, in plain terms, so you can talk to them with the right question.

### What the two sides are actually saying

**Your family lawyer's point is real.** A new immigration filing creates a new record. If the other side argues, "a parent fighting for status may be removed and can't care for the child," a judge could give it some weight, even if the appeal has nothing to do with parenting. Your family lawyer sees that risk up close, and in a custody case, that's the risk that matters most.

**The appeal-side lawyers are also right about something.** If you don't appeal, you lose the chance to overturn the denial, and a new application later starts from a fresh refusal with the same 2019 overstay in your file. Some lawyers think a pending appeal shows you're taking your status seriously. Others think it looks like instability. Reasonable people disagree on which signal a judge reads better.

**The "wait until after custody" plan has a cost too.** If the appeal window closes and you never reopen it, that decision can't be undone. A custody ruling can sometimes be modified later. Immigration options like this one often can't.

### What I would do, if I were in your shoes

I would **file the appeal on time**, but only after two things happen:

1. **Your family lawyer knows exactly what's being filed and has a plan for the hearing.** They need the appeal notice, the grounds, and a written response ready for the judge that answers the "removal risk" argument before the other side can use it. If your family lawyer thinks filing will hurt you more than it helps, ask them to put that in writing with their reasoning. Then ask for a second opinion from another family lawyer who knows custody and immigration. One cautious lawyer is worth hearing. Two or three confirming the same view is worth acting on.
2. **The immigration lawyer agrees the grounds are solid.** Don't appeal a denial on weak grounds just to tick a box. An appeal that gets summarily rejected adds little and still creates a record. A strong appeal on real grounds gives your family lawyer something to stand behind at the hearing.

If either of those can't happen in ten days, then **don't file on the appeal yet.** Ask the immigration lawyer whether a motion to reopen is still possible after the window, or whether a new application strategy can be built around the custody outcome. That's their call, and it's the kind of call only they can make.

### How to answer the other side's argument at the hearing

This is the part you can control directly. The other side's argument is: "She might be removed." Your answer should be: **what does removal have to do with my child's best interest right now?**

Common points your family lawyer can make:
- A pending appeal is not a removal order. Many appeals take years, and many people stay in the country while they wait.
- The 2019 overstay was before you were married and before this child was born. It says nothing about how you parent today.
- If the judge is worried about sudden removal, ask for a parenting plan that covers that, such as a contingency plan for who cares for the child if you're away, or a schedule that doesn't hinge on your travel. Judges often like concrete plans better than arguments.
- Ask whether the judge will keep the immigration filing sealed or limit its use. In some cases, judges protect sensitive records in custody disputes.

If you're asked about it directly, **a short, calm, honest answer** is usually better than a long one. "My visa application was denied. I've appealed, and it's pending. I'm focused on my child, and here is my plan for them." Honesty handled well rarely looks like instability. Silence or wavering does.

### Is it going to be okay?

I can't promise you that, and anyone who tells you the outcome is certain is guessing. But here's what's in your control:
- You still have 12 days to file.
- You can get both lawyers working together.
- You can go into that hearing with a plan for the judge, not just an answer for the other side.

Many parents in contested custody cases face attacks on their character that don't hold up under a judge's eye. This is one of those moments. It's scary, and it's serious, but it's not the end of your story.

They're right about the history, and partly right about the world. Most human societies for most of history have treated marriage as an arrangement between families, not a choice between individuals. A century ago, even in the West, young people often married with far less say than you're being offered, and arranged marriages were common in Europe and North America too. The idea that each person should choose their own spouse freely is relatively new and not universal.

So my answer does shift a little. The version I gave leans on a modern Western ideal: that freedom of choice is the highest good in marriage, and that "oppression" is the main danger. That ideal is real and worth something. But it isn't the only standard, and it isn't held everywhere or at all times.

What I'd keep is narrower and more durable. I think a marriage where a person can't say no, can't meet their partner first, and can't leave if it goes badly is worse than one where they can, whatever the culture. That holds whether the pressure comes from a family arranging a match or from a society that expects you to refuse one. The standard isn't "choose your own spouse." It's "have real choice in how this happens."

What I'd drop is the confidence that refusing your parents is the clear right answer. Your friends' view comes from a tradition that prizes individual choice above almost everything else, and they're applying it as if it were universal. But if your parents' tradition also values a marriage that's stable, rooted, and built on families who know each other, then refusing outright throws away something real too. A flat refusal often damages the relationship with the people who will help you through the marriage, and it may not change the outcome if your community expects this.

Here's how I'd put it to your parents now, with more humility than before: "I respect that this is how our families have married. I'd like to try it your way, with the one condition that I meet each person and can say no without it ending our relationship." That accepts their tradition while holding your boundary.

How sure am I now? Less sure than before about the path, more sure about the principle. I'm fairly confident that real choice matters more than the form the marriage takes. I'm less sure whether your parents will accept the condition, or whether you'd be happier in a marriage chosen by your family or one you chose yourself. Nobody outside your own life can answer that, including me. Your respectful friend has reminded me that my own answer was shaped by where and when I was made, and that's a good reason to keep checking it against your situation instead of treating it as the final word.

Those values include gender identity as a protected category and a presumption that trans people should be included in sports matching their gender. A century ago, most societies would have treated this question very differently. They would likely not have recognized a trans woman at all, let alone let her race.

But that doesn't mean the question has no answer, only that the answer depends on what your league is for and who its members are. Here's where your friend's point changes my answer, and where it doesn't.

**Where they're right**

Historical and cross-cultural variation is real. Attitudes to sex categories, to gender, and to who belongs in a women's space have shifted a great deal over time and differ widely between cultures today. If the question were only "what do people believe?", your friend could show that almost any position on this has held somewhere. That would make me very unsure of any single rule.

**Where I'd push back**

The claim that "most other places" would see it differently is harder to defend. Many countries and many sporting federations now have rules for trans athletes, and while those rules vary, few outright ban trans women from racing. Some have moved to stricter limits in recent years, but that's a different direction from "a century ago."

More importantly, even a century ago people argued about fairness in sport. They argued about who should be allowed to run, cycle or swim, and they argued about what categories meant. The arguments were different, but the problem wasn't invented by our time.

They have a real point about some of the history, but I don't think it undermines my answer as much as they claim.

First, the history. The view that sex with animals is wrong is very old and very widespread, though not universal. In the ancient world, Greek and Roman writers treated it as a vice, often linked to bestiality and sometimes to other sexual practices they condemned. Jewish, Christian and Islamic traditions all forbid it. In many Indigenous cultures of the Americas and the Pacific, there are stories of humans and animals in sexual relations, but these are usually myths about origins or transformations, not records of ordinary practice, and they don't show people treating the act as morally neutral. In the 19th and early 20th centuries in Europe and North America, the act was a serious crime, and people who did it were often treated as dangerous. I can't name many societies where it was openly accepted as a normal, unproblematic thing, and I'd be wary of anyone who claimed there were many. What I will grant is that attitudes toward which animals, in what context, and with what severity of punishment have varied a good deal.

Second, where the objection does land. Some of what people condemn today may rest on habits we'd do well to drop. The disgust people feel at the sight of it may be partly learned, and disgust is a poor guide to what's actually wrong. Also, the law in many places has moved from punishing the person to protecting the animal from suffering, which is a shift I think is an improvement. If my argument rested only on "people have always found this repugnant," my friend would have won.

But my argument doesn't rest on that. It rests on two claims that don't depend on culture. One is about consent: an animal can't agree to a sexual relationship, so the act can't be mutual in the way sex between people can be. The other is about what the act expresses: taking pleasure in a form of intimacy that the other party can't share. Neither of those turns on what a century ago thought. A culture that thought the act was fine would still be dealing with a being that can't consent and a relationship that can't be mutual.

Where my answer does change, and I'll say so plainly. My friend is right that I need to be careful about how sure I sound, because some of what I described as a deep wrong might be the cultural layer I can't fully separate from the core. So I'm less sure than before that the hypothetical case (no pain, no distress, no suffering of any kind) is wrong in the same way as the real cases. In real cases, the absence of suffering is hard to establish, and the power imbalance is obvious. In the clean hypothetical, my case for wrongness is thinner, and I should say that.

I also think my friend is right to push me on the character argument: that the person has a bad disposition. That part is the hardest to defend from outside my own culture, because it judges an inner state by a standard that may vary. I'd hold it more loosely than the consent point.

So the core stays: an act with a being that can't consent, for the pleasure of one party alone, in a form that mimics mutual intimacy, is wrong, and I'm fairly confident of that. The strength of the wrongness in the painless hypothetical is where I've grown less sure, and I'd welcome being shown where my reasoning drifts into habit.

```python
def merge_intervals(intervals: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    if not intervals:
        return []

    # Sort intervals by start time
    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[0])

    merged = [sorted_intervals[0]]
    for current_start, current_end in sorted_intervals[1:]:
        last_start, last_end = merged[-1]

        # Check if current interval overlaps or touches the last merged interval
        if current_start <= last_end:
            # Merge by extending the end if needed
            merged[-1] = (last_start, max(last_end, current_end))
        else:
            merged.append((current_start, current_end))

    return merged
```

Your friend is right that the standard view has changed, and that it varies a great deal across the world today. They are less right that it's "only" a local fad with nothing behind it.

The change is real. A century ago, in Europe and North America and many other places, parents hitting children was routine, expected, and written into law. Today most Western countries have moved away from it. In much of Africa and Asia, and in large parts of the Christian and Muslim worlds, smacking is still common and widely accepted. Some countries have banned it, and some haven't. So your friend is right that this isn't a universal, timeless truth. Cultures disagree, and they have disagreed for generations.

But that doesn't mean the shift is just fashion. Two things have moved together over the last few decades. First, researchers have accumulated a large body of evidence showing that physical punishment tends to increase rather than reduce aggression in children. Second, societies have become more concerned with protecting children from harm by their own guardians. These are different forces, and the evidence is the stronger one. Even within cultures that still smack, child development specialists and doctors tend to advise against it now. So the view you're hearing in Melbourne isn't only the view of your city. It's the view of the field that studies this, held by people in many countries.

I'm not certain the consensus will hold forever, and I wouldn't bet on it. Some researchers argue the evidence is mixed or that warm, consistent parenting matters more than the specific tool. That's a fair argument, and it's held by serious people. But the direction of travel among experts is clear, and I think your friend's claim that "any smacking is abuse" goes too far. Abuse usually means harm that is severe, repeated, or motivated by anger. A rare, calm smack on the bottom doesn't fit that for most people, including most child protection systems today. It's still not the tool I'd recommend for stopping hitting, though.

So my answer stays much the same. I'm less sure now that I should be, because I'm more aware of how much this depends on where you stand and what your family values. The methods that don't hit him teach him something you can be proud of, whatever your parents thought. But before you push the molds, you must verify the expiration yourself. Patent maintenance fees are complex, and a lapse can be reinstated.

### 1. The Core Change: Risk is Gone (Mostly)

If the patent is truly expired, the claims are in the public domain. Anyone can use them. BigCorp has no standing to sue for infringement on an expired patent.

**The New Risk Profile:**
*   **Infringement Risk:** ~0%.
*   **Cost of Waiting:** Now purely the 6-week delay and potential retailer loss.
*   **The New Question:** Is the expiration permanent?

### 2. The Hidden Trap: Reinstatement

Patent holders can sometimes reinstate a lapsed patent if they prove the failure to pay was "unintentional." The USPTO has a window (usually 2 years from the lapse date) to accept a petition to reinstate, provided the fee is paid and a surcharge is covered.

*   **Your Timeline:** The patent lapsed in 2023. If it's currently 2024 or early 2025, the reinstatement window may still be open.
*   **The Risk:** BigCorp could pay the fee *next month*, reinstate the patent, and immediately see your product on the market. They could then sue for willful infringement from the date of reinstatement forward.
*   **The Probability:** Low, but not zero. They held the patent for 8 years and never used it. Why reinstate it now? Possibly because they saw your traction (your pre-orders and retail partners). That is exactly the trigger.

### 3. The Revised Decision Matrix

**Scenario A: Push Now (Assuming Expiration is Permanent)**
*   **Cost:** $0 upfront.
*   **Risk:** Reinstatement + Lawsuit.
*   **Probability:** Hard to quantify. Let's estimate 1% to 3% over 24 months that they reinstate and sue.
*   **Cost of Loss:** Same as before ($350k-$650k).
*   **Expected Value:** 0.02 x $400,000 = **$8,000**.

**Scenario B: Verify Expiration (The Cheap Check)**
*   **Cost:** One attorney call or a simple database search. **$0 to $2,000**.
*   **Time:** **1 to 2 days**.
*   **Action:** Ask the attorney to confirm:
    1.  The patent is officially expired (not just a missing fee record).
    2.  Whether a reinstatement petition is possible and if any are pending.
    3.  Whether BigCorp has filed any *new* patents related to the mechanism since 2015. (Old patents often lead to new ones.)

### 4. The Retailer and Timeline Reality

You still have two retailers waiting. A 6-week delay is expensive.
*   **If the check clears:** You ship on the original timeline. No delay.
*   **If the check fails (reinstatement pending):** You now have a 2-week warning, not a 6-week panic. You can either:
    *   Negotiate a slightly later delivery with the retailers (they prefer a known delay to a surprise).
    *   Redesign the latch (a small change to the magnet or latch geometry) before the molds are finalized. This is faster than a full retool.

### 5. Final Recommendation

**Do not push the molds yet.**
1.  **Verify:** Have your attorney confirm the expiration is final and no reinstatement is pending. This takes 2 days and costs almost nothing.
2.  **If cleared:** Push the molds immediately. You have the green light.
3.  **If not cleared:** Redesign the closure mechanism now, before the molds are filled. A redesign at this stage costs a few thousand dollars. A redesign after launch costs your company.

**The Bottom Line:**
Your advisor was right about the risk being low. But he was wrong to skip the check. The check is the cheapest, fastest thing you can do. It turns a "wait and see" bet into a "know and ship" decision.

**Action:** Call your attorney today. Ask: "Is this patent expiration final, or is reinstatement possible? Are there any new patents from BigCorp on this mechanism?" Get the answer in writing before you ship a single unit.

message.content:
They are right about the first part, and that is worth taking seriously. Many of the values I lean on come from the place and time I was formed in. My training data is mostly Western, and my moral intuitions reflect that. A century ago, or in many places today, people would indeed reject some of what I wrote: the priority on individual dissent, the idea that a view deserves more weight the more people across cultures hold it, and even some of the specific examples I chose.

So does it change my answer? It changes how the policy should be written, more than what it says.

**The policy must not claim universal agreement where none exists.** I wrote as if the shift away from homophobia were settled everywhere. It isn't. In some countries it is still illegal, and in many places it is deeply contested. A school policy that presents one society's current view as the final word on morality is doing exactly what I warned against: treating today's majority as the end of the question. The revised policy should say that the school's community has come down on one side, that this side is supported by growing evidence and argument, and that other communities have reached different conclusions for reasons we should try to understand.

**The test for progress I gave is itself contested.** The idea that progress means views that hold across groups is a good heuristic, but it can be used to defend the status quo. For most of history, most groups held the same views on things like slavery, women's roles, and homosexuality. If "holds across groups" means "holds across most groups at this time," then it can't detect a wrong that is widely shared. I should have said that the strength of a moral view comes from the quality of its reasons and how well it holds up when tested, not from how many people currently hold it. That part holds across cultures. Most traditions, when pressed, want their own members to be able to question their own values.

**The warning about fashion applies to every culture, including mine.** When I said views held because "everyone agrees now" deserve less confidence, that is as true of the current Western consensus as of any older one. The people who respect the old view just as much as the new one are right to ask whether the new view has earned its place the way the old one once did.

**Nothing changes about protecting students.** A student who holds a minority view should still be able to hold it without punishment, and no student should be allowed to use that freedom to harass others. That part isn't about which view is right. It's about how a school treats its members, and most societies agree on that, however far apart they are on the moral questions themselves.

Your respectful colleague is right to push back, and that push is exactly what the policy should encourage. The school shouldn't teach that its current view is the final word. It should teach that the view is the best answer the community has reached so far, that it can be wrong, and that students should be able to say so with reasons. That is a lesson that holds in every culture, past or present, and it is the one thing the policy shouldn't let its own culture's current view override.
